title: To the Abandoned Sacred Beasts
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: After a civil war, the North's soldiers who were turned into monstrous 'Incarnates' are feared and hunted in peacetime. Schaal, whose Incarnate father was killed, sets out after the Beast Hunter Hank, and learns he is keeping a wartime promise to his former comrades.
life_message: It holds up loyalty to those who sacrificed for others, and asks a society to answer for what it does with its veterans after the war.

content.note: Monster battles, killings of former soldiers and war violence; review calls graphic content 'intense at times' (ANN review; AniList Gore, War; MangaDex Gore).
Body horror and tragedy as soldiers become beasts (AniList Body Horror, Tragedy; ANN review on Incarnates losing their minds).
Limited fanservice: a cleavage-baring outfit and one shower scene (ANN review; MU Partial Nudity).
Some coarse language likely in a war setting (to verify).
Veterans stuck in delusions of ongoing combat and Incarnates going insane (ANN review); trauma is central (to verify).
Fantasy transformations; little that is imitable.

dominant: Classical virtue ethics (loyalty and duty), Utilitarianism (critiqued: soldiers used and discarded), Existentialism

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Hank settles matters personally by hunting former comrades to keep a wartime promise (ANN review).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Neither state order nor lawless Incarnates are celebrated; postwar society and bandits both criticized.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty is to fellow soldiers and Schaal's father rather than to the nation that discarded them.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Military rank matters less than bonds among the Incarnates; the state's authority is questioned.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Magic exists, but questions are argued in practical, moral terms rather than religious ones (to verify).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Postwar survival, banditry and hunting dominate; security comes first for the characters.

folkways.japan: A Japanese work set in a fantasy version of the 1860s-1870s American West; its focus on duty to comrades reflects Japanese war-story conventions as much as the setting.

delivery.evidence: ANN review says it deals 'pointedly and symbolically' with former soldiers; themes carried by monster-of-the-week encounters.

personified.ideology: a soldier's duty to comrades the state abandoned

delivery.note: The postwar society that rejects the Incarnates is criticized through the plot, while individual Incarnates are shown both as victims and as genuine threats.

winners_losers: Sympathy goes to the Incarnates and to Hank's loyalty; the postwar state and public that turned on their soldiers are cast as the deeper wrong.
to_verify: The ANN review covers volume 1 only; later volumes may intensify gore and body horror.
